The first concerned the Arab bourgeoisie.

The Arab bourgeoisie was capable of moving into a position of dependence on imperialism because this could serve its class interests. But such a move required an ideological change. The bourgeoisie had to reshape an ideology that no longer fitted the conditions of the imperialist age.
This change therefore had to be prepared culturally. The bourgeoisie needed cultural tools that could help it rebuild its ideology.
The thinkers of rising capitalism understood that building—or rebuilding—an ideology was a complicated process. It depended on a whole network of real historical, social, and cultural relationships.
The bourgeoisie, for example, could not simply abandon its connection to its national history and national culture.

At the same time, it was not in imperialism’s interest for the bourgeoisie that depended on it in a colonized or semi-colonized country to become completely cut off from the national feelings shared by large parts of the population.
Nor was it in imperialism’s interest for this bourgeoisie to become unable to restrain those national feelings when they came into conflict with imperialist interests.

If the bourgeoisie became completely separated from the general feelings of the people, this would do more than expose its dependence on imperialism and its betrayal of national interests. It would also weaken the ability of bourgeois ideology to attract the middle social groups.

Because their class position can shift, these middle groups can sometimes serve as a reserve ideological ally of the bourgeoisie during social conflict. At other times, the bourgeoisie can lose that alliance—for example, when a national liberation struggle is rising in the country.

The thinkers of capitalism took all this into account as capitalism moved into its imperialist stage. When economic and political imperialist expansion toward the Arab region began, it had to be accompanied by a cultural and ideological approach directed at the Arab bourgeoisie.

For this purpose, imperialism needed a cultural tool connected to national history and national culture. But that history had to be interpreted in a way that was not progressive, and the culture had to be viewed through methods that suited this class-based and fatalistic interpretation.

This was the first purpose behind the imperialist attempt, through Orientalism, to influence Arab culture and shape its modern direction. The study of its intellectual heritage in general, and its philosophical heritage in particular, became one of the means by which this influence could be exercised.

The second purpose concerned the general ideological formation of those sections of Arab society that were most closely connected to culture and the intellectual heritage, and that had the greatest opportunity to shape new Arab thought: intellectuals, students, teachers, professors, writers, and researchers.

Orientalist studies of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage began to expand precisely as the imperialist age was beginning. Their dominant tendency was to emphasize the idealist and supernatural elements of that heritage above others, while relying on subjective and ahistorical methods of interpretation and analysis.

All this shows that these studies were not separate from the wider development of capitalism into its imperialist stage. Nor were they separate from the ideological preparation taking place in countries that were becoming targets of imperialist control.
The aim was to support that control with intellectual and ideological foundations built partly from the national culture and intellectual heritage of the countries themselves.

It also meant creating a body of thinkers and ideologues drawn from the local bourgeoisie, or from sections of the lower and middle bourgeoisie moving toward it. These people could then establish those ideological foundations in their own countries, using the methods and approaches introduced by Orientalist scholarship.

In fact, the methods Western Orientalists used to study our intellectual heritage greatly impressed modern Arab thinkers, writers, and researchers when they first encountered them in Western universities.

They saw methods of research that were new to them, and they were drawn to them. They began to promote these methods and criticize the formal and traditional approaches that had been used in our own countries during the early stages of the modern Arab revival.
They then moved beyond simple admiration and advocacy and began to use these methods themselves.
Ṭāhā Ḥusayn was perhaps the boldest among the generation that had studied at Western universities under leading Orientalist professors.

He applied the Orientalist method in one of the most sensitive and controversial areas possible: his study of pre-Islamic poetry. He approached that poetry with systematic doubt and emphasized the role of religious factors in producing poetry that was later attributed to the pre-Islamic period.
Although Ṭāhā Ḥusayn remained within the framework of idealist thought in this study, his first attempt to apply this method provoked a fierce reaction.

Even so, the road had begun to open. A whole generation of researchers followed, including Manṣūr Fahmī, Ismāʿīl Maẓhar, Aḥmad Amīn, Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq, ʿAlī ʿAbd al-Rāziq, and others who came with them and after them, continuing down to the present.

There is no doubt that the methods of research used by this pioneering generation of Arab scholars were a necessary revolution against the empty, backward, descriptive style that had dominated before them.
Here we can clearly recognize a positive effect of Orientalist methods in our intellectual life—if we are looking only at the practical style of research.
But the situation is different when we look at the deeper method behind that research: its intellectual and ideological outlook.

The appeal of Western Orientalist scholarship came partly from the fact that its new research methods seemed so striking and unfamiliar to Arab scholars. They impressed intellectuals and educated readers.

But this attraction also drew generations of writers and thinkers toward the intellectual and ideological content that came with those methods: toward a particular way of looking at the world, especially society and thought, and toward a particular way of looking at the national intellectual heritage and studying it.
We have already seen enough evidence of this in our earlier discussion of modern Arab writers.
This means that Orientalist studies of the heritage have served—and continue to serve—the ideological purposes built into their method.
But new developments have also appeared.

As the Arab liberation movement has developed, and as scientific socialist thought has won victories on a world scale, scientific awareness, national liberation consciousness, and class consciousness have all deepened.
This has prepared the way for a new approach to understanding the heritage: an approach based, as we said earlier, on a scientific historical method.
D — The Position of the Orientalists
To identify the main positions Orientalists have taken toward the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage, we first need to identify the major tendencies around which those positions have developed.
If we look at the earliest Orientalist studies and those that followed them, we can group their main approaches as follows.
First: the approach based on “race theory.”
This means studying the heritage from a racial point of view.

Arabs, or the “Semitic race,” or Eastern peoples in general are compared with Western peoples and described in one of several ways: as naturally and completely incapable of intellectual creativity; as capable of only one particular kind of thinking, such as analysis or synthesis, but not others; or as naturally limited to spiritual matters in the supernatural sense and incapable of dealing with material reality.
All of them are arbitrary attempts to divide the peoples of the world and rank them according to supposedly natural differences in their intellectual and cultural abilities.

The “theoretical” basis of this approach is not only unscientific. In ideological terms, it is one of the positions most hostile to the development of peoples living under imperialist domination, including the Arab people.

It directly challenges their hopes for national liberation by presenting them with what is supposed to be an inescapable wall of fate. It tells them that they cannot transform their backward conditions into more advanced ones because their weakness is built into their very nature and is therefore permanent.

The bourgeois ideological meaning of this “race theory” is also clear. It suggests that differences between human beings come from differences in their intellectual and moral nature rather than from class divisions.
This approach appears in Orientalist studies in several forms.
Heinrich Becker (1886–1933) compares the effect of the Greek cultural heritage in the East with its effect in the West.
In doing so, he presents ideas that assume a basic difference between East and West in the way they responded to ancient civilization. By “the East,” he means the Arabs in particular.

For Becker, the key difference lies in what he calls humanism: a sense of the self, or the presence of a distinctly human and subjective emotional life within a people’s cultural and civilizational production.
This becomes the decisive basis of the distinction he draws between East and West.
The East, in his view, has a rational and logical tendency but does not possess “humanism.”

The West, by contrast, had already produced the idea of humanism through Christian thought, and this humanism was bound to reappear later. In Becker’s view, it is deeply rooted in the West. It appeared in the Roman period, returned during the Renaissance, and still appears today in different forms in different European countries.
According to Becker, this “decisive difference” between East and West explains why they responded differently to the heritage of Greek civilization:

“Differences of type and race, differences in geographical environment, and the independent historical development of each side mean that the heritage of the ancients”—by which he means the Greeks and Romans—“produced in the West a form of development completely different from the one it produced in the East.”
But what was it about the heritage of the ancients that supposedly produced such different reactions?
Becker answers through Werner Jaeger, who describes humanism as:
“the idea of civilization based on the ideal of the pure cultivation and education of the human being, an ideal created by the Greeks when they reached the highest stage of their development.”
For Becker, then, humanism in this sense is the central feature of Greek civilization.
Since he believes the East lacks this humanism while the West possesses it naturally, he concludes that the two regions had to respond differently to Greek civilization.
Becker says much more along these lines.

He denies that the Arabs created a civilization of their own or added anything fundamentally new to the civilizations of the countries they conquered. He argues that practically everything remained as it had been before, except that official and administrative documents that had once been written in Greek, Persian, or Coptic were now written in Arabic, while “nothing essential in the administration itself was changed.”
In other words, Becker sees no real human creative process in the relationship between the Arabs and the civilization of the ancients.
From this point of view, the East was interested in Greek writings only when they suited what he calls its “rational and logical tendency.”
But the “Greek spirit”—by which he means humanism—remained closed to the East. This included Greek lyric poetry, imaginative literature, and everything he regarded as most purely Greek.
So, in Becker’s formulation, the Greek heritage met ideas in the East, but in the West it met human beings.
To reinforce this argument, Becker turns to Goethe’s famous statement:
“East and West can no longer be separated.”
Becker interprets this to mean that the general view of the world and of life found in East and West is fundamentally very similar because both came from the same source.
By that source he means the Greek heritage.

So even the similarity between East and West, in Becker’s view, does not come from the historically and scientifically sound fact that human societies in different ages can share common forms of thought.
Instead, the similarity comes from the claim that both Eastern and Western views of life descend from the same Greek origin.
But even this similarity is only superficial for Becker, because he still believes that East and West responded to the Greek heritage in fundamentally different ways.
The idea that one part of humanity has a special claim to rational thought or humanism while another part does not is itself an ahistorical assumption.
And because this assumption rests on an unscientific theory of race, it is false at its foundation.
Becker refers more than once in his lecture to the factor of “race.”
But both rational thought and humanism are forms of consciousness shared by humanity as a whole.

Every human society is capable, simply because it is human, of developing both forms within its social consciousness and national culture. At a particular historical moment, one may become more dominant than the other.
But what determines this balance is not race or geography.
The decisive factor is the historical situation of each society: the form of its social relationships and the psychological outlook produced by its culture as a whole.
And historical conditions are never fixed. They are always moving and changing. As they change, they inevitably change the many relationships and factors that depend on them.
Becker’s judgments, however, appear to apply equally to East and West under all conditions and in every historical period.
It is true that Becker sometimes mentions “historical factors” alongside racial ones.
But what does he mean by “historical” in the first place?
When we look at his argument as a whole, these supposed historical factors appear frozen, static, and permanent.
In that sense, they are not historical at all.
Before Becker, the French philosopher Ernest Renan (1823–1892) had already made “race theory” the direct basis of his well-known judgments about “Arab philosophy.”
Renan carried conclusions from his comparative study of the Semitic languages into his study of philosophy.
As a scholar of Semitic languages, he followed a classification common among European linguists of his time, who divided peoples into “Semitic” and “Aryan” groups.
They based this distinction on similarities they believed they had found between Sanskrit and European languages.
Peoples whose languages they traced back to Sanskrit, including groups such as the Brahmins of India, were placed within the “Aryan” family together with European peoples.
Other peoples whose languages came from different linguistic roots, including the Arabs, were placed in another human family that they called the “Semitic race.”
Renan then added something further to this linguistic classification.
He turned it into a theory of hierarchy between the two supposed racial families in terms of cultural level and intellectual ability.
He placed the “Aryan race” above the “Semitic race.”
Renan says this quite openly. He even claims that he was the first to establish that the Semitic race was inferior to the Aryan race.
This theory of hierarchy between human “races” later became part of the theoretical foundation of Hitler’s Nazi ideology, an ideology hostile both to science and to humanity.
